# kernable (CLI)

The `kernable` command runs the kernel and does everything around it: it creates keys, grants and development certificates, revokes keys, applies a service's membership, lists what is registered, checks stores, and submits single commands for scripting. `kernable` without arguments prints this page as text. The flags of `kernable start` are in [kernable start](./configuration).

Commands that take an `<addr>` talk to a running kernel. Commands that take a `<store>` open the store file directly: the ones that only read it work while the kernel runs, the ones that change it need the kernel stopped.

## Run the kernel

### `kernable start`

```text
kernable start --root <root.pub> [<flag> <value>]...
kernable start --dev [<flag> <value>]...
```

Runs the kernel in the foreground, trusting grants signed by the root keys; the flags are listed by `kernable start --help`. On Unix, SIGHUP reads the kernel key again. SIGTERM or SIGINT refuses new requests, lets running ones finish and stops; SIGTERM to a pair's primary hands its role to the standby in sync first. SIGUSR1 stops the same way, never handing over (a new binary takes the stores over). `--dev` is for trying kernable out: it creates `root.key`, `kernel.key`, `vault.key`, `app.key` and `app.grant` in the working directory if missing (app may do everything) and defaults to `--root root.pub`, `--vault-key vault.key`, `--ui-listen 127.0.0.1:7234` and `--durability` normal. With `--reader <writer>[,<writer>]` it runs as a reader, a read-only copy of the writer (started with `--readers` on): it catches up, from `--from-backup` if it is new, then answers queries from its copy and forwards commands. Exit 2 on invalid flags; exit 1 if the kernel stops on an error (a reader whose copy no longer continues its writer's log: start it again).

### `kernable demo`

```text
kernable demo [--ui-listen <addr>]
```

Runs kernable for presentations: a kernel on a new store in a temporary directory, with a small bank built in, shown step by step on the Stage at `http://<addr>/demo` (default `127.0.0.1:7234`). Reset starts again on a new store; Ctrl-C ends it and removes everything.

## Keys and trust

### `kernable keys new`

```text
kernable keys new <name>
```

Writes `<name>.key` (the secret key, readable by the owner only, never overwritten) and `<name>.pub` (the key ID), and prints the key ID.

### `kernable grant`

```text
kernable grant <root.key> <name.pub> [--succeeds <old.pub>] [--delegated] <permission>...
```

Writes `<name>.grant`, signed by the root key, and prints its permissions. A permission is `<action>=<type>,<type>`... or a bare `<type>` for every action. Actions: `submit` `run` `subscribe` `listen` `query` `answer` `check` `privileged` `vault_read` `vault_erase` `data_read` `data_write` `cache` `manage` `replicate` `read` `export` `backup` `reserved_order` `process`. A type is `*`, `<domain>.*` or `<domain>.<Type>`; manage takes service names, process takes process names (`<domain>.<name>`), privileged takes `bypass_authorization`; replicate (a standby), read (a reader), export, backup and `reserved_order` (negative listener orders, for kits) take `*`. `--succeeds` lets this key take over the aggregates and listeners registered with `<old.pub>`. A newer grant for the same key replaces the older one. `grant=<action>`,... lets a key grant those actions to others (never `*` or grant; not part of `*`). `--delegated`: `<root.key>` is such a key, not a root; its own grant (`<root>.grant` beside it) goes along, and the kernel takes the grant for those actions only.

### `kernable revoke`

```text
kernable revoke <addr> <root.key> <key.pub> <since>
```

Revokes a key for good from `<since>` on (UTC, like `2026-10-27T09:00:00Z`): the kernel refuses it, ends its connections and rejects its queued commands accepted since then (`key_revoked`). The kernel must be running.

### `kernable push-grant`

```text
kernable push-grant <addr> <name.grant>
```

Takes a grant into effect on a running kernel at once, as presenting it does. Pushing a delegate's newer grant that names fewer actions narrows what it granted: the kernel drops those grants and ends the sessions that relied on them, and passes it to its standby and readers.

### `kernable witness`

```text
kernable witness --listen <addr> --root <root.pub> --state <file> --generation <file> [--lease-ms <ms>] [--tls-...]
```

Runs the witness of a pair of kernels started with `--witness`: it decides which one is the primary, renews the primary's lease (3000 ms by default) and lets the standby in sync take its place when the lease runs out. It keeps the term and the roles in `<file>` (default witness.state); listens on `127.0.0.1:7300` by default, elsewhere only with mutual TLS (`--tls-cert`, `--tls-key`, `--tls-client-ca`). `--generation`: its generation (below), checked against the roots and sent with every answer; every witness has one.

### `kernable witness generation`

```text
kernable witness generation <root.key> <generation> <witness-address>
```

Writes witness.generation: the generation of the witness the kernels of a pair reach at `<witness-address>` (as they name it in `--witness`), signed by the root key. A new pair starts with 1, for its witness and both kernels (`--witness-generation`); a witness that replaces a lost one gets a higher one, and kernels that have seen it ignore older witnesses.

### `kernable relay`

```text
kernable relay --dir <dir> (--root <root.pub> --allow-push <key.pub>[,<key.pub>] | --access <file>) [--listen <addr>] [--tls-...]
```

Runs a relay: it keeps copies of writers' records in `<dir>` (one directory per copy), taken from pushers whose keys `--allow-push` names (kernable push), and serves each to readers (kernable start `--reader <relay>` `--reader-copy <copy>`) whose grants a `--root` signed with read. It applies and checks nothing: readers check every record against the writer's checkpoints. A relay several customers share takes `--access <file>` instead: per copy the pushers and roots it takes (`[copies.<copy>]` pushers = [...], roots = [...], key IDs), read at every check; a copy it does not name is refused. Listens on `127.0.0.1:7400` by default, elsewhere only with TLS (`--tls-cert`, `--tls-key`: a public CA's certificate serves clients with no certificate of their own, who reach it as `https://<host>:<port>`; `--tls-client-ca` adds mutual TLS).

### `kernable relay key`

```text
kernable relay key <file>
```

Writes a new copy key (hex, mode 600): the pusher seals what it sends a relay with it (`--copy-key`) and the copy's readers open it (`--reader-copy-key`). The relay never holds it: it sees records' positions, hashes and sizes, nothing else.

### `kernable push`

```text
kernable push --follow <addr>[,<addr>] --key <key> --to <relay> --copy <name> --copy-key <file> [--root <root.pub>]...
```

Follows the writer at `<addr>` (started with `--readers` on; both kernels of a pair, comma-separated) as a reader and sends every record, sealed with the copy key, to the copy `<name>` at the relay `<relay>` over a connection it opens itself, until stopped. `<key>` needs a grant for read on `*` (the grant file next to it is sent along, read again on every connection) and must be one the relay takes (`--allow-push`). The writer keeps its records until the copy holds them. Beside the push it takes the writes the copy's readers send through the relay and makes them on the writer. With `--root`, a new reader may ask it for the copy key: it seals the key for the reader's own key if a root (or the root's enrol key, granted `grant=read`) granted the reader read and nothing involved is revoked (it notes revocations as they pass, in `<copy-key>.revoked`). Connections use `KERNABLE_TLS_*`, as the SDKs do.

### `kernable partitions apply`

```text
kernable partitions apply <addr> <key> <map.json>
```

Applies a partition map on the control partition at `<addr>`: {'epoch': 2, 'partitions': {'p1': ['host:7233'], 'p2': [...]}, 'default': 'p1', 'control': 'p1', 'tenants': {'acme': 'p2'}} (JSON, with double quotes). Tenants not listed live on the default partition; the epoch must grow with every map. `<key>` needs a grant for manage on `*`. The other partitions take it from the control partition.

### `kernable partitions show`

```text
kernable partitions show <addr> <key>
```

Prints the partition map the kernel at `<addr>` holds.

### `kernable partitions move`

```text
kernable partitions move <addr> <key> <tenant> <to>
```

Moves `<tenant>` with its data to partition `<to>`: applies a map that marks it moving on the control partition at `<addr>`, waits until `<to>` has copied it, then applies the map with the tenant on `<to>`. Meanwhile the tenant's requests are answered UNAVAILABLE. Run it again to finish a move it did not. `<key>` needs manage on `*`.

### `kernable promote`

```text
kernable promote <addr> <key>
```

Makes the standby at `<addr>` (started with `--follow`) the primary: it stops following and serves. A reader is never promoted. `<key>` needs a grant for manage on `*`. Promote only a standby whose primary is gone: a primary that still runs is fenced (it tells nobody of a write from then on), and rejoins as a standby of the new one. Without a witness, a standby the primary never told it is in sync is refused: the primary may have told writes it lacks.

### `kernable switchover`

```text
kernable switchover <addr> <key>
```

Hands the primary role over to the standby in sync now: the primary at `<addr>` refuses new requests (the SDKs retry them on the other kernel), lets running ones finish, and waits until the standby holds every record (at most 10 s). In a pair (`--witness`) it tells the witness; without one it tells the standby on its stream. The standby serves at once, and the old primary stops: in a pair, started again, it follows; without a witness, it starts only with `--follow`. For updates and moves: update or start the standby, switch over, update or retire the old primary. `<key>` needs a grant for manage on `*`.

### `kernable switchover`

```text
kernable switchover --socket <admin.sock>
```

The same on the primary's local socket (`--admin-socket`), with the same checks and no key: whoever reaches the socket (the kernel's user, root) may switch over.

### `kernable certs new`

```text
kernable certs new <dir> <client>...
```

Writes a development CA (`ca.tls.crt`), a kernel certificate (`kernel.tls.crt`, `kernel.tls.key`) and a certificate per `<client>` (`<client>.tls.crt`, `<client>.tls.key`) to `<dir>`, for mutual TLS. The CA key is not kept: issue a new set to add clients. Production brings its own PKI.

## Deploy and inspect

### `kernable apply`

```text
kernable apply <addr> <key> <manifest.json> [--deployment <version>] [--wait <seconds>]
```

[--force] Applies a service's membership: a JSON manifest with service, workers, listeners, middlewares, processes, metadata and deployment (or `--deployment`): the code version that serves the service from now on. Its workers run the commands and its read models count; the other deployments' stay connected and idle. Applying an earlier deployment's membership rolls back. A process the service's membership listed before and no longer lists starts no new cases. A switch to another deployment waits until it has caught up: its listed workers connected, its listed read models within `--deployment-switch-lag` events of the head (at once for a deployment that served before). Before, it is refused (`not_caught_up`, exit code 3) naming what it waits for; `--wait` tries again for up to that many seconds, `--force` switches at once. Signed with `<key>`, whose grant needs `manage=<service>`; the grant file next to the key (`app.grant` for `app.key`) is sent along. The kernel must be running. Once per deploy.

### `kernable services`

```text
kernable services <store>
```

Lists each applied membership: the service, its metadata, who applied it and when, and the workers, listeners and middlewares it lists, marking those that never registered; then the service's dynamic listeners, registered but not listed.

### `kernable workers`

```text
kernable workers <store>
```

Lists the registered aggregate types with their command types, key, service and when a worker for them was last seen.

### `kernable listeners`

```text
kernable listeners <store>
```

Lists the registered listeners with order, position, event types, key, service, middleware and when they were last seen. A listener its service's membership does not list is marked: it counts for nobody.

### `kernable listeners parked`

```text
kernable listeners parked <store>
```

Lists the events listeners parked: the listener, position, event type, code, attempts, when, whether a retry is asked for, and the message (for a handler error only the error's type; the listener's log has the rest).

### `kernable schemas`

```text
kernable schemas <store>
```

Lists the highest stored schema version per event type.

### `kernable deployments`

```text
kernable deployments <store> [--json]
```

Lists the deployments (code versions) that wrote events or registered read models: first and last position and how many events each wrote, its read models; then the deployment each service's membership names. `--json`: {deployments: [{deployment, events, firstPosition, lastPosition, lastAt, listeners}], services: [{service, deployment}]}.

### `kernable deployments drop`

```text
kernable deployments drop --socket <path> <deployment> [--force] [--json]
```

Forgets a deployment's read model and middleware registrations (with their positions) and its snapshots while the kernel runs, through its local socket (`--admin-socket`); its events stay, the kernel logs it. Refused (exit code 3) for the deployment a membership names (serving) and for one with a worker or read model connected (running); one that wrote events (it served, a rollback may need it, and the kernel does not know an operator's grace period) only with `--force` (`served_before`). `--json`: {deployment, readModels, snapshots, forced}, or {error, message} when refused.

### `kernable deployments since`

```text
kernable deployments since <store> <position>|--at <time> [--version <v>] [--json]
```

What was written after `<position>` (or since the UTC `<time>`), to check before a rollback: per event type, schema and deployment the events and aggregates, marked NEW TYPE or NEW SCHEMA where no earlier event had them (an older deployment refuses commands on those aggregates: `unknown_history`); then scheduled commands and process timers stored since and still due, running process cases that moved, and process versions registered. `--version`: only that deployment's events. `--json`: the schema in the deployments how-to.

### `kernable processes list`

```text
kernable processes list <store>
```

Lists the registered business processes: name, newest version, state (active or removed), as whom it acts (ProcessService.Act; else `process:<name>`), and when and by which key the newest version was registered.

### `kernable processes show`

```text
kernable processes show <store> <name> [<version>]
```

Prints a process's model as registered, the newest version or `<version>`, as indented JSON. Exit 1 if there is no such process or version.

### `kernable processes cases`

```text
kernable processes cases <store> <process> [--state running|waiting|incident|ended]
```

Lists the cases of a process: tenant, case ID, state (running: a command sent or a query asked; waiting: for an event or a time; incident; ended) and the step it is at (or how it ended). Reads every event, also with the kernel stopped; the UI's Processes view shows them live.

### `kernable processes case`

```text
kernable processes case <store> <process> <case>
```

Prints a case's events as a timeline: when, version, event type and its data.

## Processes, with the kernel running

### `kernable processes retry|skip|cancel`

```text
kernable processes retry|skip|cancel <addr> <key> <process> <case> [--tenant <tenant>]
```

Resolves a case's incident: retry runs its step again, skip goes on to the step's next step, cancel ends the case (also without an incident). Signed with `<key>`, whose grant needs `process=<process>`; the grant file next to the key is sent along. `--tenant` names the case's tenant when its ID is used in several.

### `kernable processes remove`

```text
kernable processes remove <addr> <key> <name>
```

Removes a process: it starts no new cases, its running cases finish; registering it again makes it active. Signed with `<key>`, whose grant needs `process=<name>`; the grant file next to the key is sent along. Exit 1 if it was removed already.

## Parked events, with the kernel running

### `kernable listeners retry`

```text
kernable listeners retry <addr> <key> <listener> <position|--all>
```

Delivers the listener's parked event at `<position>` again, or all of them, the next time it is connected; if it fails again, it is parked again. Signed with `<key>`, whose grant needs `manage=<service>` of the listener (`manage=*` for one without a service); the grant file next to the key is sent along. Exit 1 if none of them is parked.

### `kernable listeners dismiss`

```text
kernable listeners dismiss <addr> <key> <listener> <position|--all>
```

Removes the parked event at `<position>`, or all of them, without delivering them again. Like retry otherwise.

## Check the store

### `kernable verify`

```text
kernable verify <store> <kernel.pub>...
```

Recomputes the hash chain and checks every checkpoint and signature, with every key the kernel ever had: give all its `.pub` files. Read-only, so the kernel may run. Prints the counts, `PROBLEM` and `SUSPECT` lines, then `OK` or `TAMPERED`. Exit 0: intact. Exit 1: tampered, or the check failed. Exit 2: intact, but something was signed by a key at or after its revocation (`SUSPECT` lines). Events after the last checkpoint are counted: cutting them off could not be detected.

### `kernable checkpoint`

```text
kernable checkpoint <store> <kernel.key>
```

Signs a checkpoint of the newest event now, as the running kernel does every `--checkpoint-interval-ms`. Kernel stopped.

## Export and import

### `kernable export`

```text
kernable export <addr> <key> <file>
```

Writes everything the running kernel at `<addr>` holds to `<file>`: every record of its store, every file of its data store and the vault values, which stay encrypted with its vault key. The kernel signs a checkpoint first. `<key>` needs a grant for export on `*`; the grant file next to the key is sent along. `<file>` must not exist; it is written readable by its owner only, and deleted if the export does not finish. Snapshots and the cache are not exported. Prints the counts and the kernel keys that signed the store.

### `kernable export`

```text
kernable export <file> [--store <s>] [--data-store <d>] [--vault-store <v> --vault-key <k>]
```

The same from stores read directly, kernel stopped. The flags name the stores as for kernable start, with its defaults; without `--vault-key` the vault is left out, which fails if the store refers to vault values.

### `kernable import`

```text
kernable import <file> [--store <s>] [--data-store <d>] [--vault-store <v> --vault-key <k>] [--kernel-pub <kernel.pub>]...
```

Fills new, empty stores from an export, then checks the store like verify, with the same output and exit codes. `--vault-key` must be the source's vault key. The whole file is checked before anything is written: a copy cut short or changed, or a wrong vault key, is refused. Without `--kernel-pub`, the store is checked with the kernel keys the export names; compare them with the source's `.pub` files, or name those. Keep the source's kernel `.pub` files for verify after the kernel runs on the new stores.

### `kernable import`

```text
kernable import <file> --mask-vault --vault-key <new file> [--with-files] [--store <s>] [--data-store <d>] [--vault-store <v>] [--kernel-pub <kernel.pub>]...
```

Makes a masked copy (a preview) from an export: its records without a vault value, so every personal value reads as null, as after an erasure. `--vault-key` names a file that does not exist: the copy's own, new vault key, which it writes, with a new, empty vault at `--vault-store`. Files are left out unless `--with-files`. The store is marked as a copy: a kernel runs it only alone, with that vault key.

## Previews

### `kernable copy`

```text
kernable copy <source store> --mask-vault --vault-key <new file> [--files-from <d>] [--store <s>] [--data-store <d>] [--vault-store <v>] [--kernel-pub <kernel.pub>]...
```

Makes a masked copy (a preview) of a store on this machine, read in one consistent view, also while its kernel runs (SQLite): as import `--mask-vault`, without an export file and without the source's vault or its key. `--files-from` copies the files of that data store too. Then checks the copy like verify.

## Run a node

### `kernable node join`

```text
kernable node join <url> <token> [<dir>] [--ca <pem>]
```

Links the node in `<dir>` (default .) to a control point (`--ca`: whose certificate this CA signed, trusted for it alone) with a one-time join token: makes `node.key` (unless there is one) and writes managed.toml. kernable node then pulls signed settings every 5 s and reports every 30 s. Settings set only a fixed list: the role and whom it follows (writer, standby, reader of a writer or of a copy), the relay and copy a writer pushes to, the kernel version (`versions/<v>/kernable`), a reader's maximum lag and a pair's witness; never keys, grants, secrets or services. Settings with anything else, not signed by the settings key pinned at the join, for another node or older than those held are refused.

### `kernable node`

```text
kernable node <project.toml>
```

Runs one node of a project: the kernel and, with a [backup] section, the backup follower, with a [push] section the pusher to a relay, as child processes it restarts when they exit. It reads the file again when it changed (it looks twice a second) or on SIGHUP, and restarts a child whose command changed or whose binary was replaced (a kernel hands its stores over to the new one). SIGTERM or SIGINT stops the children (SIGKILL after stop-seconds, default 30). The file has [kernel] (flags: the flags of kernable start without their dashes, env, binary, image, cpus, memory, stop-seconds), [backup] (to, key, backup-key, follow, segment-seconds, base-hours, keep, check-hours, signer, cpus, memory, env), [push] (to, copy, key, copy-key, root, follow, cpus, memory, env), [pair] (witness, node-key, advertise, peer, kernel-keys, standby-timeout-ms, witness-generation: this node's kernel of a pair), [node] (instance, project, podman, metrics-listen: GET /metrics, cpus and `memory:` the instance's total, network: own, the default, or host), any number of [[secret]] (name, and file or command) and any number of [[service]] (name, build, file, command, key, env, secrets, cpus, memory, stop-seconds, writable, expose): containers built with podman on the node, rebuilt on SIGHUP, run after the kernel with `KERNABLE_URL`, `KERNABLE_INSTANCE` and their key. Every child's output comes out of the node prefixed with its name. Paths are relative to its directory. Exit 2 if the file is invalid at start.

### `kernable expose`

```text
kernable expose <socket>=<host:port>... Passes every connection to each Unix socket on to its
```

address, both ways: a node runs it in an instance's pod, for a service's port to be reached through the socket.

## Continuous backup

### `kernable backup key`

```text
kernable backup key <file>
```

Writes a new backup key (32 random bytes in hex) to `<file>`, readable by its owner only; never overwrites one. Keep it apart from the backups, as you keep the root key: without it a backup cannot be read.

### `kernable backup`

```text
kernable backup --follow <addr>[,<addr>] --key <key> --to <target> --backup-key <file> [--segment-seconds <s>] [--base-hours <h>] [--keep <n>] [--check-hours <h>] [--status-file <file>] [--signer <url>] [--signer-key <file>]
```

Follows the kernel at `<addr>` (started with `--backup` on; both kernels of a pair, comma-separated) and writes its records to `<target>`, encrypted with the backup key, until stopped: a base, then a segment every `--segment-seconds` (default 5) or 16 MiB, a new generation every `--base-hours` (default 24), the newest `--keep` (default 7) kept. `<key>` needs a grant for backup on `*`; the grant file next to it is sent along. `<target>` is `file:<dir>` or `s3://<bucket>/<prefix>`, with `KERNABLE_S3_ENDPOINT`, `KERNABLE_S3_REGION`, `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` and `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`. Vault values stay encrypted with the kernel's vault key besides. With `--check-hours`, it also checks the backup that often, as backup check does, and logs what it found. With `--status-file`, it notes there (JSON) when it last uploaded, up to which record, and when it last checked and what it found. With `--signer <url>` (or `KERNABLE_S3_SIGNER`), an s3:// target needs no credentials: for every request it asks the signer for a presigned one, signed with `<key>` (or `--signer-key`, `KERNABLE_S3_SIGNER_KEY`); `KERNABLE_S3_SIGNER_CA` names the CA certificates the signer's certificate is checked against. While the target or its signer fails, it logs an error, tries again, and the kernel keeps the records.

### `kernable backup list`

```text
kernable backup list <target> --backup-key <file> [--signer <url> --signer-key <file>]
```

Prints the generations of a backup: each base's record and time, how far its segments reach, and the vault key its vault values are sealed with (a generation has one; a kernel whose vault key changed begins a new one).

### `kernable backup plan`

```text
kernable backup plan <target> --backup-key <file> [--at <time> | --at-record <n>] [--json <file>] [--signer <url> --signer-key <file>]
```

Prints what a restore to that point builds from (the generation and its vault key) and the erasures the backup holds after it: committed later, they are undone by such a restore. `--json` writes the same as JSON.

### `kernable backup check`

```text
kernable backup check <target> --backup-key <file> [--signer <url> --signer-key <file>]
```

Reads the newest generation all through, without writing a store: every object opens with the key and decodes, and the records chain from the base to the last segment. Prints the record a restore reaches and how old it is; exits 1 if the backup does not check out.

### `kernable restore`

```text
kernable restore <target> --backup-key <file> [--at <time> | --at-record <n>] [--reapply-erasures <file>] [--mask-vault [--with-files]] [--signer <url> --signer-key <file>] [--store <s>] [--data-store <d>] [--vault-store <v> --vault-key <k>] [--kernel-pub <kernel.pub>]...
```

Fills new, empty stores from a backup: the newest generation that begins before `--at` (UTC, like `2026-11-04T13:40:00Z`) or `--at-record`, its base, then its segments up to there (default: everything), then checks the store like verify, with the same output and exit codes. `--vault-key` must be the source's vault key of that generation's time; the flags name the stores as for kernable start. Without `--kernel-pub`, the store is checked with the kernel keys the backup names. To a point, it first lists the erasures committed after it: restored as it was, they did not happen yet. To apply them again, `--reapply-erasures <file>` (or yes when asked) writes them to `<file>` for kernable erasures apply. With `--signer` and `--signer-key`, it reads an s3:// target through a signer, as backup list, plan and check do. With `--mask-vault`, and `--vault-key` naming a file that does not exist yet, it makes a masked copy (a preview) as import `--mask-vault` does, with the files only if `--with-files`; no vault key of the source is needed.

### `kernable backup signer`

```text
kernable backup signer --listen <addr> --to s3://<bucket>/<prefix> --allow <key.pub>[,<key.pub>] [--expires-seconds <s>]
```

A reference backup signer: answers the signer protocol over plain HTTP on `<addr>` with requests presigned with the credentials of the environment (as for an s3:// target), valid for `--expires-seconds` (default 300), for that prefix and those below it, to the keys `--allow` names. For tests and trusted networks; a signing service keeps the credentials away from the machines it signs for.

### `kernable erasures apply`

```text
kernable erasures apply <addr> <key> <file>
```

Submits again each erasing command of the list restore `--reapply-erasures` wrote, signed with `<key>` (granted submit for those commands), its context kept: the kernel commits new erasing events and erases the values. Exit 1 if one is rejected or cannot be sent.

## Maintenance, with the kernel stopped

### `kernable listeners remove`

```text
kernable listeners remove <store> <name>
```

Removes a listener and its middleware, so they no longer count. If a listener connects again under that name, it starts at the newest event. Exit 1 if there is no such listener.

### `kernable deployments drop`

```text
kernable deployments drop <store> <deployment> [--snapshots <url>] [--force] [--json]
```

Forgets a deployment's read model and middleware registrations (with their positions) and its snapshots (default store: next to `<store>`); its events stay. A read model of it that connects again rebuilds from the start. Refused as with `--socket`: never the serving deployment, one that served before only with `--force`. While the kernel runs, use `--socket`.

### `kernable workers remove`

```text
kernable workers remove <store> <domain.Aggregate>
```

Unregisters an aggregate type: its commands are refused (`NOT_FOUND`) unless a membership lists it. Exit 1 if there is no such aggregate.

### `kernable vault rekey`

```text
kernable vault rekey <vault> <old.key> <new.key>
```

Re-encrypts every vault value with a new key; then start the kernel with `--vault-key <new.key>`. `<vault>` is the `--vault-store`, for example `sqlite:vault.db`. A key encrypts at most 2^32 values (each with a random nonce): the kernel warns at startup past half of that and refuses new values at the limit, until the vault is rekeyed.

## Scripting

### `kernable`

```text
kernable --version
```

Prints the version, the system and the architecture.

### `kernable submit`

```text
kernable submit <addr> <client.key> <tenant> <domain> <aggregate_type> <aggregate_id> <command_type> <payload>
```

Signs a command with a new ID and submits it, waiting until it has settled; the grant file next to the key is sent along. `<payload>` is sent as given, usually JSON. Prints the command ID, then a committed line per event with its global position, version, type and payload, or rejected `<code>`: `<message>` with exit 1. It cannot seal vault fields: not for commands with personal or secret values.

## kernable Cloud

### `kernable cloud login | logout | whoami | teams | members | tokens | projects | audit`

```text
kernable cloud login | logout | whoami | teams | members | tokens | projects | audit
```

Signs in to a kernable Cloud installation by device code and manages its teams, members, CI tokens and projects and reads a team's audit log through its account API (`--api <url>`); kernable cloud help lists them all.

## Arguments and exit codes

`<addr>` is `host:port`, `http://host:port`, or `unix:<path>` on Unix. To reach a kernel over mutual TLS, set `KERNABLE_TLS_CA`, `KERNABLE_TLS_CERT` and `KERNABLE_TLS_KEY` to PEM files, as for the SDKs. `<store>` is the kernel's `--store`: `sqlite:<path>`, a bare SQLite path, or `file:<path>`. Exit codes, unless a command says otherwise: 0 success, 1 failure, 2 unknown command or wrong arguments.
